text: Semantic HTML elements like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <footer> improve accessibility and SEO by describing content meaning instead of just layout.
Use <button> for clickable actions and <a> for navigation. Avoid <div onclick=...>, since a div isn't keyboard-focusable or accessible by default.
Always include an alt attribute on tags describing the image for screen readers. Use alt="" for purely decorative images so screen readers skip them.
The CSS box model consists of content, padding, border, and margin, in that order from the inside out.
box-sizing: border-box makes an element's width and height include its padding and border, which is usually more predictable than the default content-box behavior.
Flexbox (display: flex) is ideal for one-dimensional layouts, a single row or column, while CSS Grid (display: grid) is designed for two-dimensional layouts with both rows and columns.
CSS specificity is calculated from IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then elements/pseudo-elements, in that priority order. Inline styles and !important override normal specificity.
CSS custom properties, written as --variable-name, let you define reusable values and update them dynamically at runtime, unlike Sass variables which are compiled away.
SCSS is a superset of CSS that adds nesting, variables, mixins, and functions, then compiles down to plain CSS that browsers can read.
SCSS nesting lets you write .card { .title { ... } } instead of repeating .card .title everywhere, but nesting more than 2-3 levels deep usually hurts specificity and maintainability.
SCSS mixins, defined with @mixin and used with @include, let you reuse a block of styles with parameters, useful for things like repeated media queries or vendor prefixes.
Media queries, like @media (max-width: 768px) { ... }, apply different CSS rules based on the viewport size, forming the basis of responsive design.
Mobile-first CSS means writing your base styles for small screens first, then using min-width media queries to layer on styles for larger screens.
The <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> tag is required for a responsive page to actually render at the correct scale on mobile devices.
CSS position: relative positions an element relative to its own normal position, while position: absolute positions it relative to its nearest positioned (non-static) ancestor.
z-index only has an effect on elements with a position value other than static, and it only compares stacking order within the same stacking context.
CSS Grid's grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) creates three equal-width columns that share the available space evenly.

The :hover, :focus, and :active pseudo-classes let you style interactive states; :focus-visible specifically targets keyboard-only focus, which is better for accessibility than styling all focus the same way.
Form inputs should use <label for="id"> paired with the input's matching id attribute, so screen readers correctly announce the label when the field receives focus.
CSS transitions (e.g. transition: all 0.3s ease) animate property changes smoothly, while @keyframes with the animation property give finer control over multi-step animations.
The rem unit is relative to the root element's font-size, while em is relative to the parent element's font-size, which makes rem more predictable for consistent spacing across a page.
Using a CSS reset or a library like normalize.css at the start of a project removes inconsistent default styling that browsers apply differently out of the box.
JavaScript variables declared with let and const are block-scoped, while var is function-scoped — this is why using var inside loops can lead to unexpected bugs.
const doesn't make an object immutable — it only prevents reassigning the variable itself. You can still mutate the properties of an object declared with const.
The === operator checks both value and type, while == performs type coercion first, which is why === is generally the recommended comparison operator.
Arrow functions don't have their own 'this' binding — they inherit 'this' from the surrounding lexical scope, unlike regular functions.
A Promise represents a value that will be available now, later, or never, and has three states: pending, fulfilled, and rejected.
async/await is syntactic sugar built on top of Promises, letting asynchronous code read like synchronous code while staying non-blocking.
Array methods like .map(), .filter(), and .reduce() return new arrays or values without mutating the original array, unlike .push() or .splice() which mutate in place.

The event loop processes the call stack first, then microtasks like resolved Promises, then macrotasks like setTimeout — which is why a resolved Promise callback runs before a setTimeout callback even with a 0ms delay.
Closures let an inner function keep access to variables from its outer function's scope even after that outer function has already returned.
JSON.stringify() converts a JavaScript object into a JSON string, and JSON.parse() converts a JSON string back into a JavaScript object.
The spread operator (...) can copy the properties of an array or object into a new one, which is useful for creating shallow copies without mutating the original.
Destructuring assignment lets you extract values from arrays or properties from objects into separate variables in one line, e.g. const { name, age } = user.
The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree representation of an HTML page that JavaScript can read and modify to change what's actually displayed in the browser.
document.querySelector() returns the first element matching a CSS selector, while document.querySelectorAll() returns a NodeList of every matching element.
Event delegation means attaching one event listener to a parent element instead of separate listeners to many children, relying on event bubbling to catch child events.
try/catch blocks let you handle runtime errors gracefully instead of letting an unexpected error crash the entire script.
Template literals, written with backticks, support multi-line strings and ${expression} interpolation, unlike regular single- or double-quoted strings.
The 'use strict' directive enables strict mode, which catches common coding mistakes like accidental global variables and throws errors instead of failing silently.
Array.isArray() is the reliable way to check whether a value is an array, since typeof returns 'object' for arrays too.
Debouncing delays a function call until after a pause in incoming events (like typing), while throttling limits a function to run at most once per fixed time interval (like scrolling).
ES modules, using import and export, let you split code across separate files with explicit dependencies, gradually replacing older patterns like CommonJS require() even in browser code.
The nullish coalescing operator (??) returns its right-hand value only when the left side is null or undefined, unlike || which also triggers on any falsy value like 0 or an empty string.
React components are reusable, self-contained pieces of UI written as functions that return JSX, which looks like HTML but actually compiles down to JavaScript function calls.
JSX requires a single root element per component return — or you can use a React Fragment, written as <>...</>, to group elements without adding an extra DOM node.
Props are read-only data passed from a parent component down to a child. A child component should never modify its own props directly.
The useState hook returns a current state value and a setter function; calling the setter triggers a re-render of the component with the updated value.
The useEffect hook runs side effects, like data fetching or subscriptions, after render, and its dependency array controls exactly when the effect re-runs.
An empty dependency array in useEffect ([]) means the effect runs only once after the initial render, similar to componentDidMount in older class components.
Returning a cleanup function from useEffect, such as removing an event listener, lets you clean up properly before the component unmounts or before the effect re-runs.
React requires a unique 'key' prop when rendering a list of elements, so it can efficiently track which items changed, were added, or were removed between renders.
Lifting state up means moving shared state to the closest common ancestor component, so multiple sibling components can read and update it through props.
The Context API, via createContext and useContext, lets you share data across many components without manually passing props through every level in between ('prop drilling').
Controlled components keep a form input's value in React state, updating it via an onChange handler, so React remains the single source of truth for that input's value.
The useRef hook creates a mutable reference that persists across renders without causing a re-render when it changes, often used to directly access a DOM node.
React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props haven't changed, which can help optimize expensive components.
The useMemo hook memoizes a computed value between renders, while useCallback memoizes a function reference, both helping avoid unnecessary recalculation or child re-renders.
Custom hooks are just JavaScript functions whose names start with 'use' and that can call other hooks internally, letting you extract and reuse stateful logic across components.
React's virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI; React diffs it against the previous version to calculate the minimal set of real DOM updates needed.
Conditional rendering in JSX is commonly done with a ternary operator (condition ? <A/> : <B/>) or the && operator for simple show/hide logic.
React Router's <Route> and <Link> components enable client-side navigation between views without triggering a full page reload.
State updates in React are asynchronous and may be batched, so you shouldn't rely on reading the updated state value immediately after calling its setter within the same function.
useReducer is an alternative to useState for managing more complex state logic, using a reducer function in a pattern similar to Redux.
Error boundaries are class components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree and render a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.
React's Strict Mode, via <React.StrictMode>, intentionally double-invokes certain functions in development to help surface side-effect bugs early. It has no effect in production builds.
Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser using Google's V8 engine, enabling server-side scripts, command-line tools, and build tooling.
Node.js is single-threaded but uses an event loop with non-blocking I/O, so it can handle many concurrent connections efficiently for I/O-heavy workloads like web servers.
npm (Node Package Manager) installs and manages third-party packages listed in package.json, while package-lock.json pins the exact installed versions for reproducible installs.
The require() function loads modules using the older CommonJS system synchronously, while newer Node.js versions also support the ES module import/export syntax.
process.env gives access to environment variables, commonly used to store configuration like API keys or database URLs outside of the source code itself.
Express.js is a minimal web framework for Node.js that simplifies routing, middleware, and request/response handling when building APIs and servers.
Express middleware functions run in order for each incoming request and can modify the request or response, or end the request-response cycle, using the (req, res, next) => {...} signature.
npm scripts defined in package.json's "scripts" field, like "start" or "test", can be run with `npm run <script-name>` as convenient shortcuts for common commands.
Node's built-in fs module provides both synchronous methods, like fs.readFileSync, and asynchronous ones, like fs.promises.readFile, for reading and writing files.
A Node.js process can crash entirely on an uncaught exception, which is why production apps typically use a process manager like PM2 to automatically restart the app on failure.
RESTful API design in Express typically maps HTTP methods to actions: GET to read data, POST to create it, PUT or PATCH to update it, and DELETE to remove it.
Environment-specific configuration, like development versus production settings, is often handled with .env files loaded via a package like dotenv, and kept out of version control.
Node.js's built-in http module can create a basic web server without any framework at all, but most real-world projects use Express or a similar framework for convenience.
npm's semantic versioning ranges, like ^1.2.3 versus ~1.2.3, control how much a dependency is allowed to auto-update: ^ permits minor and patch updates, while ~ permits only patch updates.
Middleware for parsing JSON request bodies in Express, express.json(), must be registered before the route handlers that actually need to read from req.body.
Node.js streams let you process data, like a large file, in smaller chunks rather than loading the entire thing into memory at once.
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) errors happen when a browser blocks a frontend from calling an API hosted on a different origin. Express apps commonly fix this with the cors middleware package.
Callbacks, Promises, and async/await are the three main patterns for handling asynchronous operations in Node.js, with async/await generally being the most readable for sequential async logic.
A package.json's "main" field specifies the entry file used when your package is imported elsewhere, while "dependencies" versus "devDependencies" separates runtime needs from development-only tools.
Node.js debugging can use console.log for quick checks, or the built-in inspector via `node --inspect` together with Chrome DevTools or an editor like VS Code for real breakpoint debugging.
Rate-limiting middleware, like express-rate-limit, protects an API from abuse by capping how many requests a single client can make within a given time window.
Node.js's cluster module, or an external process manager, can run multiple instances of an app across CPU cores, since a single Node.js process only uses one core by default.
Drupal function names should use lowercase snake_case, prefixed with the module's machine name, e.g. mymodule_form_alter().
Hook implementations must be named exactly hook_NAME() with the module's machine name replacing 'hook', for example mymodule_form_alter() implements hook_form_alter().
Drupal coding standards require 2-space indentation (no tabs) and require braces on their own line for control structures in PHP, layering Drupal-specific rules on top of PSR-12.
All classes in Drupal custom code should have full docblocks describing their purpose, and all public methods should document their parameters and return types.
Never concatenate user input directly into SQL queries in Drupal — always use the Database API with placeholders to prevent SQL injection.
Output text through Twig's automatic escaping or Drupal's Xss::filter() functions to prevent stored or reflected XSS from user-supplied content.
State-changing routes, like POST, PATCH, or DELETE actions, should require a CSRF token, which Drupal generates automatically for routes marked with _csrf_token: 'TRUE'.
Forms built with Drupal's Form API automatically get CSRF protection via a hidden form_token field, but custom AJAX endpoints need equivalent protection added manually.
Store secrets like API keys in environment variables or in settings.local.php, which should be gitignored, rather than hardcoding them in the settings.php file committed to the repository.
Always check the current user's permissions, e.g. via \Drupal::currentUser()->hasPermission(), before performing a privileged action in custom Drupal code.
N+1 query patterns, loading entities one at a time inside a loop, can severely degrade performance in Drupal — load multiple entities in bulk with the entity storage's loadMultiple() method instead.
Drupal's render cache system can cache rendered markup based on cache tags and cache contexts, avoiding redundant re-rendering of content that hasn't actually changed.
Adding proper cache tags to a custom render array ensures cached content gets correctly invalidated whenever the underlying data it depends on changes.
Enabling CSS and JavaScript aggregation in a production Drupal site reduces the number of HTTP requests needed to load a page's front-end assets.
Using a caching layer like Redis or Memcache as Drupal's cache backend significantly reduces database load compared to the default database-based cache backend.
Custom Drupal modules need a .info.yml file declaring the module's name, type, core_version_requirement, and any dependencies on other modules.
Plugin classes in Drupal, such as block plugins or field formatters, typically live under a module's src/Plugin/ directory and use annotations or PHP attributes to register themselves with Drupal.

Drupal's dependency injection container lets services be injected into a class via a static create() factory method instead of calling the global \Drupal:: helper directly, which is preferred for testability.
Configuration schema files, under a module's config/schema/ directory, define the structure and data types for that module's configuration, enabling validation and translation support.
Drupal's Entity API lets custom modules define entirely new content entity types with their own fields, in a similar way to how core Node and Taxonomy Term entities work internally.
Update hooks, named hook_update_N(), run automatically during deployment via `drush updb` to apply incremental database schema changes for a module.
Views field plugins, defined under a module's src/Plugin/views/field/ directory, let custom code add new displayable fields to the Views UI.
